knowledge_point.title: Identifying the Horizontal Shift of a Horizontally Stretched Tangent or Cotangent Curve

question.:question/problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186184149/plots/08bdf71bc37205d6c329466c-prompt.png)

The graph above shows the function $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+C),$ where $C$ is a constant. Given that $-\frac{\pi }{2}<C<\frac{\pi }{2},$ what is the value of $C?$ The dashed curve is $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{x}{2}).$ The horizontal displacement between the two marked zeros is $\frac{2\pi }{11}$ units to the left.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The parameter $C$ determines a horizontal shift of $-2C$ units, modulo the period $2\pi$.

First, we rewrite the function by factoring the horizontal stretch factor, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+C) \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{1}{2}(x+2C))\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $x+2C$ indicates that the graph of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{1}{2}(x+2C))$ is a horizontal translation of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{x}{2}).$ Comparing the two graphs below allows us to determine the amount of this shift.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186184149/plots/08bdf71bc37205d6c329466c-solution.png)

From the diagram, we see that our curve has been obtained by shifting $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{x}{2})$ by $\frac{2\pi }{11}$ units to the left. Therefore:

$$
2C=\frac{2\pi }{11}\,⟹\,C=\frac{\pi }{11}
$$

Since $-\frac{\pi }{2}<C<\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $\frac{\pi }{11}$ is in this interval, the value of $C$ is $\frac{\pi }{11}.$

$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186184149/plots/0a39dcfc0cb119000442ce5f-prompt.png)

The graph above shows the function $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{3x}{2}+C),$ where $C$ is a constant. Given that $-\frac{\pi }{2}<C<\frac{\pi }{2},$ what is the value of $C?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The parameter $C$ determines a horizontal shift of $-\frac{2C}{3}$ units, modulo the period $\frac{2\pi }{3}$.

First, we rewrite the function by factoring the horizontal stretch factor, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{3x}{2}+C) \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{3}{2}(x+\frac{2C}{3}))\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $x+\frac{2C}{3}$ indicates that the graph of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{3}{2}(x+\frac{2C}{3}))$ is a horizontal translation of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{3x}{2}).$ Comparing the two graphs below allows us to determine the amount of this shift.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186184149/plots/0a39dcfc0cb119000442ce5f-solution.png)

From the diagram, we see that our curve has been obtained by shifting $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{3x}{2})$ by $\frac{2\pi }{5}-\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{\pi }{15}$ units to the right. Therefore:

$$
\frac{2C}{3}=-\frac{\pi }{15}\,⟹\,C=(-\frac{\pi }{15})(\frac{3}{2})\,⟹\,C=-\frac{\pi }{10}
$$

Since $-\frac{\pi }{2}<C<\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $-\frac{\pi }{10}$ is in this interval, the value of $C$ is $-\frac{\pi }{10}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{2x}{5}+C) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{2}{5}(x+\frac{5C}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $x+\frac{5C}{2}$ indicates that the graph of $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{2}{5}(x+\frac{5C}{2}))$ is a horizontal translation of $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{2x}{5}).$ Comparing the two graphs below allows us to determine the amount of this shift.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186184149/plots/b03964b9f82b020fb6cee65e-solution.png)

$$
\frac{5C}{2}=\frac{10\pi }{9}\,⟹\,C=(\frac{10\pi }{9})(\frac{2}{5})\,⟹\,C=\frac{4\pi }{9}
$$

Since $-\frac{\pi }{2}<C<\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $\frac{4\pi }{9}$ is in this interval, the value of $C$ is $\frac{4\pi }{9}.$
